source: Newell, Shaw, Simon (1956) The Logic Theory Machine (read via Wikipedia Logic Theorist page, secondary)
finding: First heuristic theorem-proving program. It searched for proofs of propositional theorems in Principia Mathematica using rules of thumb (heuristics), coded in IPL. It found a shorter proof of theorem 2.85 than Russell and Whitehead.
numbers: Proved 38 of the first 52 theorems of PM chapter 2. Hand-simulated Jan 1956, program shown summer 1956.
limits: Only a secondary page was read, not the 1956 paper. The journal rejected the new proof as not notable.
agent_relevance: Founding case for search plus heuristics over proofs. Our agent should treat proof search as guided search with a checker, not free generation.

source: Davis (1954) Presburger arithmetic program on JOHNNIAC (read via Wikipedia Automated theorem proving, secondary)
finding: First program to prove a theorem by machine: a decision procedure for Presburger arithmetic (addition only), run on JOHNNIAC.
numbers: Example result reported: the sum of two even numbers is even.
limits: Secondary page. Decidable fragment only; full first-order logic is only semi-decidable.
agent_relevance: Decidable fragments can be solved exactly by code. Route such tasks to a solver, not the model.

source: Robinson (1965) A machine-oriented logic based on the resolution principle, JACM 12(1) 23-41 (read via Wikipedia Resolution page, secondary)
finding: One inference rule plus unification, applied to clauses (Skolemised conjunctive normal form). Sound and refutation-complete: a clause set is unsatisfiable iff the empty clause is derivable. Unification removes the need to enumerate ground instances, which Davis-Putnam 1960 required.
numbers: Paper pages 23-41. Factoring is part of the rule and needed for completeness.
limits: 1965 paper not opened. The secondary page does not give strategies or complexity bounds.
agent_relevance: A single mechanical rule with a completeness guarantee: when it returns a refutation, the answer is exact. Good model for a Verify step on exact tasks.

source: Gilmore (1960) and Davis-Putnam (1960) ground-instance methods (read via Wikipedia, secondary)
finding: Early first-order provers generated ground instances and tested propositional unsatisfiability (Gilmore used disjunctive normal form). This blows up combinatorially, which unification later fixed.
numbers: No numbers on the page.
limits: Secondary. Hao Wang 1960 results were not on the page and are unverified here.
agent_relevance: Naive generate-and-test dies from blowup. Instances should be created on demand, guided by the goal.

source: McCune (1997) Solution of the Robbins problem, J. Automated Reasoning 19(3) (read via Wikipedia Robbins algebra, secondary)
finding: The equational prover EQP, written by McCune at Argonne, proved that Robbins algebras are Boolean algebras. The question was open since the 1930s (Huntington 1933 axioms, Robbins soon after). Winker had done earlier work that the proof built on.
numbers: Run took eight days. NYT report 10 Dec 1996. Dahn (1998) simplified the machine proof.
limits: Secondary page; the paper PDF was not reachable (404/403). Setup needed human insight from Winker's work.
agent_relevance: An exact search can settle a hard open question when a human supplies the right reduction. Use model or human for the reduction, the prover for the check.

source: Wikipedia: Automated theorem proving, CASC and TPTP
finding: Annual CASC competition ranks first-order provers on the TPTP library. Vampire has won the first-order-formula division regularly since 2001; Waldmeister won the unit-equality division 14 years in a row (1997-2010).
numbers: Provers named: E, Otter/Prover9, SETHEO, Vampire, SPASS, Waldmeister. Propositional logic is co-NP-complete; first-order valid formulas are enumerable but invalid ones are not always recognised.
limits: Secondary page, first 100000 of 120153 characters read.
agent_relevance: Symbolic provers are mature and strong on exact first-order tasks. Call them as tools; the model translates the task into their input language.

source: Polu, Sutskever (2020) Generative language modeling for automated theorem proving (GPT-f)
finding: First transformer prover to have proofs accepted into a main proof library. The language model proposes proof steps in Metamath; best-first search by log-probability, plus a learned value function trained on its own generated statements.
numbers: Held-out Metamath set.mm: 56.22% closed vs 21.16% prior best (MetaGen-IL). 160M raw data 29.22%; 700M augmented 31.58%; policy+value with a=32 56.50% (+9.2 from more search). Model size correlated with success.
limits: Metamath only, many data choices, large test-time compute.
agent_relevance: Test-time search budget plus a checker lifts success a lot. Supports verify-and-retry loops with a hard budget.

source: Lample et al. (2022) HyperTree Proof Search for neural theorem proving
finding: AlphaZero-style search over proof hypertrees (a goal splits into several subgoals that must all be solved), with a critic and online training on unproved theorems. Tested in Metamath, Lean, and a synthetic Equations environment.
numbers: Metamath: 65.4% held-out with HTPS alone vs 56.5% GPT-f; 82.6% with online training. Lean miniF2F-curriculum 31% to 42%; 58.6% cumulative on miniF2F-valid; 41.0% pass@64 on miniF2F-test vs 36.6% GPT-f.
limits: Online training saw valid statements, so valid numbers are partly seen; test numbers are the clean ones. Heavy compute.
agent_relevance: The AND-OR structure of subgoals maps onto our subgoal library: all children must close, any alternative may close a node.

source: Zheng, Han, Polu (2022) miniF2F: a cross-system benchmark for formal Olympiad-level mathematics
finding: 488 formal problems (244 valid, 244 test) from AIME, AMC, IMO and course material, in Metamath, Lean, partial Isabelle and HOL Light. It became the standard yardstick.
numbers: Baseline at release: GPT-f on Metamath Pass@1 1.3%, Pass@8 1.6% on test. Prior rates quoted: CoqGym 30.0%, GPT-f Metamath 56.22% on its own set.
limits: Statement formalisation choices affect difficulty. Later work nearly saturates it (see a25).
agent_relevance: Benchmark contamination risk: public problems can sit in model training data.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo: theorem proving with retrieval-augmented language models
finding: Open Lean toolkit and 98,734-theorem benchmark. ReProver retrieves accessible premises (hard negatives from the same file) and feeds them to a tactic generator inside best-first search.
numbers: Pass@1 random split: ReProver 51.2%, no-retrieval 47.6%, GPT-4 zero-shot 29.0%. novel_premises split: ReProver 26.3%. miniF2F 26.5%, ProofNet 13.8% (48 of 349). Accessible-premise filter cut candidates from 128K to 33K. Training about five days on one GPU.
limits: Large drop on novel_premises shows reliance on premises seen in training. Pass@1 is not comparable with Pass@64 numbers of others.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of relevant prior lemmas helps, but generalisation to unseen lemmas is much weaker. A subgoal library helps most on familiar structure.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Thor: wielding hammers to integrate language models and automated theorem provers
finding: The language model chooses when to call Sledgehammer (symbolic premise selection plus ATP/SMT) in Isabelle. The hybrid beats either alone.
numbers: PISA: LM alone 39.0%, Sledgehammer alone 25.7%, union 48.8%, Thor 57.0%; 8.2% of problems solved only by the hybrid. miniF2F 29.6% to 29.9%. Premise-selection steps advanced the proof 1.9% of the time vs 28.2% for steps without premises.
limits: Gain small on miniF2F.
agent_relevance: Model plus exact tool beats both. Use code tools for what they do exactly, the model for choosing when.

source: Mikula et al. (2023) Magnushammer: a transformer-based approach to premise selection
finding: A contrastively trained retriever replaces hand-built Sledgehammer premise selection.
numbers: PISA 59.5% vs Sledgehammer 38.3%; miniF2F 34.0% vs 20.9%. Combined with a LM prover, PISA state of the art 57.0% to 71.0% with 4x fewer parameters. Beats Sledgehammer with 4K training examples (0.1% of data).
limits: Isabelle only; depends on the library.
agent_relevance: Learned retrieval of premises is data efficient and strong. Learning goes to retrieval; verification stays exact.

source: First, Rabe, Ringer, Brun (2023) Baldur: whole-proof generation and repair with large language models
finding: Generate the entire proof at once from a fine-tuned LLM, then repair using the proof assistant error message. No step-wise search.
numbers: PISA proof rate: Sledgehammer 25.6%; search-based LM 39.0%; Baldur 8b 40.7% with 64 samples; 8b with context 47.5% (64); 62b with context 47.9%; Baldur plus Thor 65.7%.
limits: Isabelle/HOL, one benchmark. A repair-model row in the table scored 34.8% at 16 samples, so repair effect needs care.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: revise from the real failing output of the checker. More samples and context helped clearly.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove: guiding formal theorem provers with informal proofs
finding: The LLM writes an informal proof, turns it into a formal sketch with gaps, then an automated prover closes each gap. The sketch splits the problem into easier subgoals.
numbers: miniF2F test: Sledgehammer 20.9%, Thor 29.9%, Thor+expert iteration 35.2%, DSP 39.3% with human proofs; 35.3% with Codex proofs; 37.7% with Minerva 62B; 38.9% with Minerva 540B. Valid 42.6%. 200 of 488 proved. Ablations cost 2.8 to 9.0 points. Of 50 informal proofs checked by hand, 29 (58%) were correct.
limits: Bigger informal-proof model gave only small test gains. Informal proofs are often wrong yet sketches still work.
agent_relevance: Draft, sketch, then exact closure of each gap is the closest published pattern to our subgoal library plus Verify.

source: Ding et al. (2024) PutnamBench: evaluating neural theorem-provers on the Putnam competition
finding: Hard undergraduate benchmark: 1692 formalisations of 640 theorems (Lean 4, Isabelle, Coq subset). At release almost nothing was solved.
numbers: Lean 4 (640): GPT-4 1, COPRA 1, ReProver 0. Isabelle: GPT-4 1, DSP 4, Sledgehammer 3. Coq (412): GPT-4 1, COPRA 1, Tactician 0, CoqHammer 0.
limits: Early 2024 snapshot. Later systems rose sharply (a19, a20). GPT-4 kept writing Lean 3 syntax.
agent_relevance: Format and syntax failures dominate for general LLMs; a checker shows them immediately.

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5
finding: Whole-proof Lean 4 model with SFT, RL from proof-assistant feedback, and tree search (RMaxTS) with intrinsic reward.
numbers: miniF2F-test: V1 50.0%, V1.5-RL 60.2% whole-proof; 51.6% at 128 samples in another row; best with tree search 63.5%. ProofNet-test 25.3% best (23.7% whole proof).
limits: Rows use different sample-budget definitions; read the table before comparing.
agent_relevance: RL with a proof checker as reward works because the signal is exact. The same logic supports verifier-gated loops.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Goedel-Prover
finding: Autoformalise Numina problems into 1.64M Lean statements, then expert-iterate: each prover generation proves more, proofs join the training set.
numbers: SFT on over 800K solved statements: 57.6% miniF2F Pass@32, 7.6 points above DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5; PutnamBench 7 problems at Pass@512 (first on leaderboard then).
limits: Faithfulness of autoformalised statements is checked by LLMs, not guaranteed.
agent_relevance: Data from exact verification is the scalable resource. A wrong statement still verifies, so check the statement too.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Kimina-Prover Preview
finding: RL-trained 72B model writes long reasoning inside the Lean proof (a formal reasoning pattern) instead of tree search.
numbers: miniF2F-test 80.74% at pass@8192; 52.94% at pass@1; 68.85% at pass@32. Performance rose with model size (1.5B, 7B, 72B), unlike earlier provers.
limits: Preview release; large budget for the top number.
agent_relevance: Long reasoning before the formal step plus a checker gives strong low-budget results. Budget matters: 28 points between pass@1 and pass@8192.

source: Ren et al. (2025) DeepSeek-Prover-V2
finding: Recursive pipeline: DeepSeek-V3 decomposes a theorem into subgoals, a small prover proves each, and the pieces are stitched into cold-start data for RL.
numbers: 671B: miniF2F-test 82.4% at pass@32, 88.9% at pass@8192 (217/244). ProofNet-test 37.1% at pass@1024. PutnamBench 47 of 658. ProverBench AIME 24-25: 6 of 15 formal vs 8 of 15 for DeepSeek-V3 informal majority vote.
limits: Authors say the formal-informal gap is narrowing, not closed. Large sample budgets.
agent_relevance: Subgoal decomposition, per-goal proving, then stitching is the subgoal-library idea with a measured benefit.

source: ByteDance Seed (2025) Seed-Prover: deep and broad reasoning for automated theorem proving
finding: Lemma-style whole-proof model that refines proofs from Lean feedback, proved lemmas and self-summaries; light, medium, heavy test-time settings; Seed-Geometry engine for geometry.
numbers: Past IMO (155 problems) 78.1%; miniF2F-test 99.6%; PutnamBench 331 of 657 (light setting 201); CombiBench 30.0% vs 10.0% prior; MiniCTX-v2 81.8% vs 44.3% (o4-mini). IMO 2025: 4 of 6 in contest, 5 of 6 after deadline; humans formalised the statements.
limits: Heavy setting is very expensive; statements were formalised by people.
agent_relevance: Lemma reuse plus iterative repair against the checker scales. More compute on the same loop took Putnam from 201 to 331.

source: Chervonyi et al. (2025) Gold-medalist performance in solving Olympiad geometry with AlphaGeometry2
finding: Neuro-symbolic: a symbolic deduction engine (DDAR) plus a Gemini model proposing auxiliary constructions, with several search trees sharing facts.
numbers: IMO-AG-50 solved: AG2 42, AG2 single tree 38, AG1 27, average gold medalist 40.9, DDAR alone 16 (AG1 DDAR 14); OpenAI o1 0 and Gemini thinking 0. IMO-AG-30: AG2 30, AG1 25, gold 25.9. Language coverage 66% to 88%; solve rate 84% vs 54%.
limits: Geometry only; needs formalised input; 88% coverage limit.
agent_relevance: The symbolic engine does the exact deduction, the model only proposes constructions. Direct template for our Propose and Verify split.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: logical inference via neurosymbolic computation
finding: The LLM translates text to first-order logic; Prover9 decides. Ten samples with majority vote over prover outputs; syntax errors filtered.
numbers: FOLIO: StarCoder+ 56.0% vs CoT 41.8%; GPT-3.5 62.6% vs 54.9%; GPT-4 LINC below CoT, not significant (McNemar p=0.58). ProofWriter: GPT-3.5 96.4%, GPT-4 98.3% with LINC. FOL syntax errors: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4.
limits: Failure modes: missing implicit facts (e.g. Person(Harry)), syntax errors such as one symbol with two arities. ProofWriter is synthetic and easy to translate.
agent_relevance: A prover only checks what the translation says. Translation fidelity is the weak link; guard it with held-out checks (G3).

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers
finding: The LLM formalises the problem, a solver (Prover9 and others) infers, and solver error messages drive a self-refinement loop.
numbers: Average +39.2% over standard prompting and +18.4% over chain-of-thought across ProofWriter, PrOntoQA, FOLIO, LogicalDeduction, AR-LSAT. GPT-4 ProofWriter 52.67 standard / 68.11 CoT / 79.66 Logic-LM; FOLIO 69.11 / 70.58 / 78.92.
limits: Some problems are not executable and need a fallback. FOLIO gain for GPT-4 is smaller than on synthetic sets. Model column assignment inferred from table layout.
agent_relevance: Solver error text is a clean, code-located signal for revision, in line with G2.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: effect of search budget on pass rates
finding: Across provers, pass rate climbs with the number of sampled attempts, so reported numbers are not comparable without the budget.
numbers: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B 82.4% (pass@32) to 88.9% (pass@8192); Kimina 52.94% (pass@1) to 80.74% (pass@8192); GPT-f +9.2 points from more search; Baldur 8b 40.7% at 64 samples.
limits: Cost per attempt differs a lot between systems.
agent_relevance: Report cost with accuracy. Retry budgets pay only when a checker exists.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: benchmark saturation
finding: miniF2F went from 1.3% (GPT-f Metamath pass@1, 2021) to 99.6% (Seed-Prover, 2025). PutnamBench went from 1 of 640 (GPT-4, 2024) to 331 of 657 (2025).
numbers: Putnam: 1 (GPT-4) -> 7 (Goedel SFT) -> 47 (DeepSeek V2) -> 331 (Seed).
limits: Public benchmarks; training-data overlap not ruled out by these papers. Lean version and statement fixes change counts.
agent_relevance: Fast gains came from RL on exact checking and compute. Expect any exact-check domain to saturate quickly.

source: Cross-paper synthesis: failure and boundary cases
finding: Generalisation to new lemmas is weak, general chat models fail on formal syntax, and informal reasoning without a checker is often wrong.
numbers: LeanDojo novel_premises 26.3% vs random 51.2%. PutnamBench GPT-4 1/640. DSP: 29 of 50 informal proofs correct. o1 and Gemini thinking solved 0 of 50 IMO geometry problems in the AG2 table.
limits: Early models; o1 geometry 0 reflects a setup without a symbolic engine.
agent_relevance: Exact tasks should always route through a formal checker. Do not trust unchecked proof text.
